steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on conditional sampling in diffusion models, framed through Doob's h-transform, with motif scaffolding for protein design as the main application. Explain why conditioning matters for proteins, review existing conditioning approaches, and list our contributions.

- Conditioning for protein design: motif scaffolding and why it is hard
- Existing approaches to conditional sampling
- Our work: Doob's h-transform and amortised training; experiments
- Contributions list

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Denoising diffusion models are a powerful class of generative models. In them, noise is gradually added to the data samples until they converge to pure noise, and then the time-reversal of this noising process lets us turn noise into samples. This has been very successful for generating high-quality images, and more recently it has also shown promise for designing protein backbones, which were validated in experimental protein design workflows.

What is important for protein design is that diffusion models let us subject this time-reversed sampling process to a target condition. For proteins a key condition is that a structural motif is included which gives the protein a particular function, like binding to a specific target or forming an enzyme active site. But for these motifs to be foldable and stable, they often have to be integrated into a larger protein structure. There have been notable successes in scaffolding some motifs experimentally, but many are still challenging to scaffold. Because of this, developing better conditional generation methods for diffusion models is an active area of research, and recently there have been several contributions from the computer vision, molecular and protein design communities.

For example, several methods treat the conditional sampling problem as an inverse (posterior sampling) problem and add a guidance term to the drift of the time-reversal (Fig. 1 c). Another line of work focuses on 'inpainting' and replaces the observed variable in the diffused state (Fig. 1 b). Other work again does heuristic conditional training with the target variables in place.

- Our work
  - reinterpret conditioning with Doob's h -transform
  - theoretical backing for existing approaches; leads to new method: amortised training (Fig. 1 d, Algorithm 5)
  - straightforward implementation; proof of concept in image generation
  - motif scaffolding: merits and shortcomings of amortised training
  - amortised training version of small-scale diffusion model Genie (cite); RFDiffusion benchmark + new benchmark dataset based on SCOPe classification (cite)
- Contributions
  - i) formal framework for conditioning diffusion processes via Doob's h -transform (Section 2)
  - ii) taxonomy of existing methods (Table 1)
  - iii) taxonomy shows a missing method -> develop and implement it (Section 2.3)
  - iv) empirical assessment on image generation and protein design (Section 3)
  - v) plug-and-play algorithms for various conditioning schemes (Appendix B)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Denoising diffusion models are a powerful class of generative models. In them, noise is gradually added to the data samples until they converge to pure noise, and then the time-reversal of this noising process lets us turn noise into samples. This has been very successful for generating high-quality images, and more recently it has also shown promise for designing protein backbones, which were validated in experimental protein design workflows.

What is important for protein design is that diffusion models let us subject this time-reversed sampling process to a target condition. For proteins a key condition is that a structural motif is included which gives the protein a particular function, like binding to a specific target or forming an enzyme active site. But for these motifs to be foldable and stable, they often have to be integrated into a larger protein structure. There have been notable successes in scaffolding some motifs experimentally, but many are still challenging to scaffold. Because of this, developing better conditional generation methods for diffusion models is an active area of research, and recently there have been several contributions from the computer vision, molecular and protein design communities.

For example, several methods treat the conditional sampling problem as an inverse (posterior sampling) problem and add a guidance term to the drift of the time-reversal (Fig. 1 c). Another line of work focuses on 'inpainting' and replaces the observed variable in the diffused state (Fig. 1 b). Other work again does heuristic conditional training with the target variables in place.

In this work we reinterpret the conditioning problem using Doob's h -transform. This new perspective gives theoretical backing to the existing approaches, and it leads us naturally to a novel method that we call amortised training (Fig. 1 d, Algorithm 5). We show that our theoretical framework is straightforward to implement and practically useful by applying it to problems, first in image generation as a proof of concept. After that we look in more detail at the merits and shortcomings of the new amortised training method for the motif scaffolding problem in protein design. For this we compare an amortised training implementation of the small-scale diffusion model Genie on the RFDiffusion benchmark and also on a new benchmark dataset we propose, which is based on the SCOPe classification.

Our main contributions are:

- i) We derive a formal framework for conditioning diffusion processes with Doob's h -transform (Section 2).

- ii) We use the framework to make a taxonomy of existing methods (Table 1).

- iii) The taxonomy showed that a specific method was missing from the current literature, so we developed and implemented this novel approach (Section 2.3).

- iv) We assess these different approaches empirically on image generation and protein design (Section 3).

- v) Finally, we give plug-and-play algorithms for implementing various conditioning schemes (Appendix B).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Denoising diffusion models are a powerful class of generative models in which noise is gradually added to data samples until they converge to pure noise. The time-reversal of this noising process then allows us to transform noise into samples. This process has been widely successful in generating high-quality images [1] and has more recently shown promise in designing protein backbones that were validated in experimental protein design workflows [2].

Importantly for protein design, diffusion models allow this time-reversed sampling process to be subjected to a target condition. For proteins, a key condition is the inclusion of a structural motif that grants the protein a particular function, such as binding to a specific target or forming an enzyme active site. For these motifs to be foldable and stable, however, they often need to be integrated into a larger protein structure. While there have been notable successes in scaffolding some motifs experimentally, many still prove challenging to scaffold [2]. This makes the development of better conditional generation methods for diffusion models an active area of research, with several recent contributions from the computer vision, molecular and protein design communities.

For instance, several methods cast the conditional sampling problem as an inverse (posterior sampling) problem and propose adding a guidance term to the drift of the time-reversal (Fig. 1 c) [3,4]. Another line of work, focusing on 'inpainting', suggests replacing the observed variable in the diffused state (Fig. 1 b) [5,6,7]. Yet other work performs heuristic conditional training with the target variables in place [2,8].

In this work, we reinterpret the conditioning problem by leveraging Doob's h -transform. This new perspective provides theoretical backing to existing approaches and naturally leads us to propose a novel method, which we call amortised training (Fig. 1 d, Algorithm 5). We highlight the straightforward implementation and practical use of our theoretical framework by applying it to problems, first as a proof of concept in image generation. We then study the merits and shortcomings of our newly proposed amortised training method in more detail for the motif scaffolding problem in protein design, comparing an amortised training implementation of the small-scale diffusion model Genie [9] on the RFDiffusion benchmark as well as on a newly proposed benchmark dataset based on the SCOPe classification [10].

Our main contributions are as follows:

- i) We derive a formal framework for conditioning diffusion processes using Doob's h -transform (Section 2).

- ii) We use our framework to create a taxonomy of existing methods (Table 1).

- iii) Our taxonomy revealed the absence of a specific method in the current literature, prompting us to develop and implement this novel approach (Section 2.3).

- iv) We empirically assess these different approaches on image generation and protein design (Section 3).

- v) Finally, we present plug-and-play algorithms to implement various conditioning schemes (Appendix B).
